stem: Which statement best describes the difference between word embeddings and contextual embeddings?

options.text: Word embeddings assign the same vector to a token regardless of surrounding text, while contextual embeddings produce different vectors for the same token depending on its context.
Word embeddings are always larger in dimension than contextual embeddings, making them more accurate for all natural language tasks.
Contextual embeddings are only used for image recognition tasks, while word embeddings handle text classification exclusively.
Word embeddings are computed at inference time for every sentence, while contextual embeddings are pre-trained once and remain fixed forever.

correct_answer: Word embeddings assign the same vector to a token regardless of surrounding text, while contextual embeddings produce different vectors for the same token depending on its context.

stem: A developer notices the word "bank" in "river bank" and "savings bank" receives identical vectors in their system. What type of embedding is most likely in use?

options.text: Contextual embedding from a transformer model, because transformers always collapse synonyms into the same vector space.
Static word embedding (such as Word2Vec or GloVe), because these assign one fixed vector per token regardless of surrounding context.
Sentence-level embedding, because sentence models always ignore individual word meaning in favour of overall tone.
Binary embedding, because one-hot encodings produce identical vectors for tokens that appear with similar frequency.

correct_answer: Static word embedding (such as Word2Vec or GloVe), because these assign one fixed vector per token regardless of surrounding context.

stem: In a RAG pipeline, why are contextual embeddings preferred over static word embeddings for encoding document chunks?

options.text: Contextual embeddings are smaller in file size, making the vector store cheaper to host on cloud infrastructure.
Contextual embeddings capture meaning that depends on surrounding words, so semantically similar passages map to nearby vectors even when they use different vocabulary.
Static word embeddings cannot be stored in vector databases, because those databases require floating-point numbers above a certain precision threshold.
Contextual embeddings are generated faster than static embeddings at query time, reducing overall retrieval latency significantly.

correct_answer: Contextual embeddings capture meaning that depends on surrounding words, so semantically similar passages map to nearby vectors even when they use different vocabulary.

stem: Which of the following is the most accurate description of how contextual embeddings are produced?

options.text: A lookup table maps each word to a pre-assigned vector that was set manually by linguistic experts during the model design phase.
Each token's vector is computed by the model during a forward pass, taking into account all other tokens in the input sequence at that moment.
The entire document is compressed into a single number that represents its overall topic, which is then expanded back to a vector by the retrieval layer.
Contextual embeddings are produced by averaging the pixel values of a visual representation of the text rendered in a fixed font size.

correct_answer: Each token's vector is computed by the model during a forward pass, taking into account all other tokens in the input sequence at that moment.

stem: Why is document chunking necessary before embedding documents for a RAG system?

options.text: Embedding models have a maximum input length (context window), so documents longer than that limit must be split into smaller pieces before encoding.
Vector databases can only store integers, so text must be broken into single characters before being converted to numeric form.
Chunking removes duplicate sentences from the document, which would otherwise cause the cosine similarity score to exceed 1.0.
Chunking is required only for images and audio; plain text documents can always be embedded whole without any size constraints.

correct_answer: Embedding models have a maximum input length (context window), so documents longer than that limit must be split into smaller pieces before encoding.

stem: A team uses very large chunk sizes (e.g. 2000 tokens per chunk) in their RAG system. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: Each chunk covers a broad topic area, so retrieved chunks contain the relevant answer but also carry significant irrelevant content, reducing generation quality.
The vector store becomes unable to compute cosine similarity, because large vectors always produce a similarity score of exactly zero.
The embedding model automatically truncates each chunk to 10 tokens, discarding the rest without warning the developer.
Large chunks improve precision by ensuring every possible answer is always present in at least one retrieved document.

correct_answer: Each chunk covers a broad topic area, so retrieved chunks contain the relevant answer but also carry significant irrelevant content, reducing generation quality.

stem: What is the trade-off when using very small chunk sizes (e.g. one sentence per chunk) in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: Small chunks increase retrieval precision for specific facts but may lose surrounding context that is needed to interpret the retrieved sentence correctly.
Small chunks always improve both precision and recall simultaneously, making them the universally optimal choice for all RAG applications.
Small chunks cause the embedding model to produce vectors of lower dimensionality, which degrades similarity search across the entire corpus.
Small chunks are incompatible with FAISS and other approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, requiring exact search instead.

correct_answer: Small chunks increase retrieval precision for specific facts but may lose surrounding context that is needed to interpret the retrieved sentence correctly.

stem: Which chunking strategy would best preserve the semantic coherence of each chunk for a document structured with clear headings and sections?

options.text: Fixed-size character chunking splits the document every 500 characters regardless of sentence or paragraph boundaries.
Structure-aware chunking splits at section boundaries (headings, paragraphs), keeping each section together as one chunk.
Random chunking selects arbitrary start and end positions to avoid any bias introduced by document formatting.
Token-count chunking always produces the best semantic coherence because it aligns exactly with the embedding model's training distribution.

correct_answer: Structure-aware chunking splits at section boundaries (headings, paragraphs), keeping each section together as one chunk.

stem: What does a vector database primarily store and index?

options.text: High-dimensional numeric vectors (embeddings) along with associated metadata, indexed for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search.
Raw text documents stored in B-tree indexes, identical to a relational database but with an additional full-text search column.
Binary image files encoded as base-64 strings, with an inverted index mapping pixel intensities to document identifiers.
SQL table schemas and foreign key relationships, optimised for join operations across normalised relational tables.

correct_answer: High-dimensional numeric vectors (embeddings) along with associated metadata, indexed for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search.

stem: Why is a vector database more suitable than a traditional relational database for semantic search?

options.text: Relational databases cannot store any numeric data, making them unsuitable for holding floating-point embedding vectors of any dimension.
Vector databases provide approximate nearest-neighbour indexes that efficiently find semantically similar items in high-dimensional space, which SQL WHERE clauses cannot do.
Traditional relational databases are limited to storing a maximum of 100 rows, making them impractical for document collections of any meaningful size.
Vector databases automatically translate natural language queries into SQL, eliminating the need for any query language knowledge.

correct_answer: Vector databases provide approximate nearest-neighbour indexes that efficiently find semantically similar items in high-dimensional space, which SQL WHERE clauses cannot do.

stem: In a RAG system, at what stage is the vector database queried?

options.text: During the fine-tuning phase, to supply training examples that update the LLM's weights based on retrieved document content.
At query time, after the user's question is embedded, to retrieve the document chunks whose vectors are most similar to the question vector.
During the tokenisation step, to replace rare tokens with semantically equivalent common tokens before the text reaches the model.
Only during the initial corpus ingestion phase; once indexing is complete the vector database is no longer accessed.

correct_answer: At query time, after the user's question is embedded, to retrieve the document chunks whose vectors are most similar to the question vector.

stem: Which of the following is an example of a vector database?

options.text: MySQL — a relational database management system with support for ACID transactions and foreign key constraints.
Pinecone — a managed vector database designed for storing and querying high-dimensional embedding vectors at scale.
Redis — an in-memory key-value store used primarily for caching and session management in web applications.
Apache Kafka — a distributed event-streaming platform used for real-time data pipelines and message queuing.

correct_answer: Pinecone — a managed vector database designed for storing and querying high-dimensional embedding vectors at scale.

stem: What does cosine similarity measure between two vectors?

options.text: The angle between two vectors, reflecting how similar their directions are regardless of their individual magnitudes.
The straight-line distance between the tips of two vectors measured in Euclidean space, penalising differences in both direction and length.
The number of dimensions in which both vectors have identical values, expressed as a percentage of total dimensions.
The ratio of the longer vector's magnitude to the shorter vector's magnitude, normalised to a scale between zero and ten.

correct_answer: The angle between two vectors, reflecting how similar their directions are regardless of their individual magnitudes.

stem: Why is cosine similarity generally preferred over Euclidean distance for comparing text embeddings?

options.text: Cosine similarity is insensitive to the magnitude of vectors, so two documents on the same topic score similarly even if one is much longer than the other.
Euclidean distance always produces negative values for high-dimensional vectors, making ranking results in ascending order impossible.
Cosine similarity can only be computed on binary vectors, making it faster than Euclidean distance for floating-point embeddings.
Euclidean distance requires all vectors to have unit norm, a constraint that embedding models cannot satisfy during training.

correct_answer: Cosine similarity is insensitive to the magnitude of vectors, so two documents on the same topic score similarly even if one is much longer than the other.

stem: Two embeddings have a cosine similarity of 0.95. What does this indicate?

options.text: The two texts are highly semantically similar, with their embedding vectors pointing in nearly the same direction in the high-dimensional space.
The two texts are completely unrelated, because a score close to 1.0 means the vectors are perpendicular to each other.
The embedding model failed to encode the texts correctly, because valid similarity scores must always be negative for natural language.
Exactly 95 percent of the tokens in both texts are identical, measured by direct character comparison of the original strings.

correct_answer: The two texts are highly semantically similar, with their embedding vectors pointing in nearly the same direction in the high-dimensional space.

stem: When would Euclidean distance be preferred over cosine similarity for a vector search task?

options.text: When the magnitude of vectors carries meaningful information (e.g. term frequency in a bag-of-words model) and should influence the similarity score.
When the vectors are derived from transformer models, because those models always produce unit-norm outputs that break cosine similarity.
When the corpus contains fewer than 100 documents, because cosine similarity is undefined for small collections.
Euclidean distance is never appropriate for any natural language processing task involving high-dimensional vectors.

correct_answer: When the magnitude of vectors carries meaningful information (e.g. term frequency in a bag-of-words model) and should influence the similarity score.

stem: Why does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) produce more accurate answers than simply stuffing an entire knowledge base into the LLM context window?

options.text: RAG retrieves only the most relevant passages, keeping the context focused and avoiding the accuracy degradation and cost that come with very long prompts.
Context stuffing causes the LLM to rewrite the knowledge base from scratch each time, which introduces random errors not present in the original documents.
RAG compresses each document into a single token before sending it to the model, reducing the prompt length without losing any information.
Context stuffing is always more accurate than RAG; RAG is only used when the knowledge base is too large to fit in any available context window.

correct_answer: RAG retrieves only the most relevant passages, keeping the context focused and avoiding the accuracy degradation and cost that come with very long prompts.

stem: A company has a 50,000-page legal document library. Why is context stuffing an impractical strategy for answering queries over this library?

options.text: The combined token count of 50,000 pages far exceeds any current LLM context window, and even partial stuffing costs orders of magnitude more than retrieval per query.
Legal documents use specialised vocabulary that LLMs are incapable of processing, regardless of how many pages are included in the context.
Context stuffing is limited to a maximum of 10 documents per prompt by the OpenAI API terms of service, making large libraries impossible to query.
LLMs automatically reject prompts containing legal text because of built-in safety filters that prevent processing of confidential documents.

correct_answer: The combined token count of 50,000 pages far exceeds any current LLM context window, and even partial stuffing costs orders of magnitude more than retrieval per query.

stem: What is "context injection" in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: The step where retrieved document chunks are inserted into the LLM prompt alongside the user's question, providing factual grounding for the response.
A security attack where a malicious user embeds hidden instructions in a document to override the LLM's system prompt.
The process of updating the LLM's weights with new knowledge by running a specialised fine-tuning loop on retrieved documents.
A compression algorithm that reduces the size of retrieved chunks by removing stop words before they are sent to the language model.

correct_answer: The step where retrieved document chunks are inserted into the LLM prompt alongside the user's question, providing factual grounding for the response.

stem: Which of the following is a key limitation of an LLM that RAG is specifically designed to address?

options.text: LLMs have a fixed knowledge cutoff date and cannot access information about events or documents that post-date their training, which retrieval from a live knowledge base resolves.
LLMs cannot process text longer than 10 tokens, so RAG breaks every query into single words before sending them to the model one at a time.
LLMs always output identical responses to identical prompts, and RAG adds randomness by shuffling retrieved chunks before injection.
LLMs are unable to generate text in any language other than English, and RAG translates retrieved passages into English before context injection.

correct_answer: LLMs have a fixed knowledge cutoff date and cannot access information about events or documents that post-date their training, which retrieval from a live knowledge base resolves.

stem: Which sequence correctly describes the components of a RAG pipeline in the order they execute?

options.text: LLM generation → vector search → document chunking → embedding → context injection
Document chunking → embedding → vector store indexing → query embedding → vector search → context injection → LLM generation
Context injection → vector store indexing → query embedding → document chunking → LLM generation → embedding
Query embedding → LLM generation → document chunking → vector search → embedding → context injection

correct_answer: Document chunking → embedding → vector store indexing → query embedding → vector search → context injection → LLM generation

stem: In a RAG pipeline, what is the purpose of the retriever component?

options.text: The retriever generates the final answer by summarising retrieved passages using a sequence-to-sequence model trained on question-answer pairs.
The retriever searches the vector store for the document chunks most semantically similar to the embedded user query and returns them for context injection.
The retriever splits raw documents into fixed-size chunks and assigns each chunk a unique integer identifier before embedding begins.
The retriever fine-tunes the embedding model on newly added documents to keep the vector representations current with the latest knowledge.

correct_answer: The retriever searches the vector store for the document chunks most semantically similar to the embedded user query and returns them for context injection.

stem: What distinguishes a RAG system from a system that only uses an LLM without retrieval?

options.text: A RAG system augments the LLM's prompt with dynamically retrieved external knowledge at query time, allowing it to answer questions beyond its training data.
A RAG system replaces the LLM entirely with a search engine, so no language model is involved in generating the final answer.
A RAG system fine-tunes the LLM on every new document as it is added to the knowledge base, keeping the model weights continuously updated.
A RAG system limits the LLM to producing outputs of exactly 100 tokens to ensure retrieved context always fits within the response length.

correct_answer: A RAG system augments the LLM's prompt with dynamically retrieved external knowledge at query time, allowing it to answer questions beyond its training data.

stem: Why is evaluation an important step in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: Evaluation measures whether the retriever is returning relevant chunks and whether the LLM is generating accurate, grounded responses, guiding iterative improvement.
Evaluation is required by law in all countries before any AI system can be deployed, regardless of the use case or risk level.
Evaluation automatically retrains the embedding model when retrieval accuracy falls below a threshold, without any human intervention.
Evaluation converts the vector store into a relational database format so that retrieved results can be audited using standard SQL queries.

correct_answer: Evaluation measures whether the retriever is returning relevant chunks and whether the LLM is generating accurate, grounded responses, guiding iterative improvement.

stem: What is the fundamental difference between a workflow and an AI agent?

options.text: A workflow executes a pre-defined sequence of steps determined at design time, while an AI agent autonomously decides its own next action at runtime based on its observations.
Workflows can only run on cloud servers, while AI agents are restricted to local machines without internet access.
A workflow uses machine learning models for every step, while an AI agent relies exclusively on hard-coded if-else rules with no learned components.
AI agents always run faster than workflows because they skip validation steps that workflows require for safety compliance.

correct_answer: A workflow executes a pre-defined sequence of steps determined at design time, while an AI agent autonomously decides its own next action at runtime based on its observations.

stem: A scheduled Python script runs every night at 2 AM, fetches sales data, and emails a report. Is this an AI agent?

options.text: Yes, because it operates automatically without a human pressing a button each time it runs.
No, because a schedule is not autonomy — the script's actions are fully determined at design time and no model chooses the next step.
Yes, because any script that interacts with external APIs qualifies as an agent under the standard definition.
No, but only because it lacks a graphical user interface; adding a dashboard would make it an agent.

correct_answer: No, because a schedule is not autonomy — the script's actions are fully determined at design time and no model chooses the next step.

stem: For which type of task is a workflow more appropriate than an AI agent?

options.text: Extracting a fixed set of fields from invoices and inserting them into a database — a well-defined, repeatable process with no decision-making required at runtime.
Researching a novel scientific topic across multiple sources, synthesising findings, and deciding which experiments to prioritise next.
Operating a customer support chatbot that must handle unpredictable questions and escalate to a human when it detects frustration.
Writing and debugging code autonomously in response to a high-level specification that may change during execution.

correct_answer: Extracting a fixed set of fields from invoices and inserting them into a database — a well-defined, repeatable process with no decision-making required at runtime.

stem: Which of the following best describes the ReAct (Reason + Act) pattern used in AI agents?

options.text: The agent alternates between reasoning steps (thinking about what to do) and action steps (calling tools or APIs), iterating until it reaches a satisfactory answer.
The agent reacts to user input by immediately generating the final answer without any intermediate reasoning or tool use.
The agent uses a pre-compiled decision tree to map every possible input to a pre-determined output without any runtime computation.
The agent runs two separate models in parallel — one for reasoning and one for acting — and combines their outputs using a voting mechanism.

correct_answer: The agent alternates between reasoning steps (thinking about what to do) and action steps (calling tools or APIs), iterating until it reaches a satisfactory answer.

stem: What is function calling (tool use) in the context of large language models?

options.text: A capability that allows an LLM to signal that it wants to invoke a specific external function, with structured arguments, so that the application can execute it and return the result.
A Python feature that allows one function to call another function directly inside the LLM's neural network weights during the forward pass.
A method for users to manually type function signatures into the chat interface so the LLM learns new skills during the conversation.
An API endpoint that replaces the LLM entirely with a deterministic calculator for arithmetic operations, improving numerical accuracy.

correct_answer: A capability that allows an LLM to signal that it wants to invoke a specific external function, with structured arguments, so that the application can execute it and return the result.

stem: Why are tools essential for agentic AI systems?

options.text: Tools extend the agent's capabilities beyond text generation by allowing it to take actions in the real world — searching the web, reading files, calling APIs, or running code.
Tools are required because LLMs cannot generate any text without first receiving a structured JSON input from an external tool call.
Tools allow the agent to bypass its context window limit by storing the entire conversation history in an external database that replaces the model's memory.
Tools are only used during the training phase to generate synthetic data; they are disconnected from the model during inference.

correct_answer: Tools extend the agent's capabilities beyond text generation by allowing it to take actions in the real world — searching the web, reading files, calling APIs, or running code.

stem: When an LLM invokes a tool using function calling, what happens next in the agent loop?

options.text: The application executes the function with the provided arguments, appends the result to the conversation, and sends the updated context back to the LLM for the next step.
The LLM executes the function internally within its neural network and generates the result without any involvement from the external application.
The conversation ends immediately and the function result is returned directly to the user without the LLM seeing or processing it.
The tool call is logged but not executed until a human operator reviews and approves it through a separate approval interface.

correct_answer: The application executes the function with the provided arguments, appends the result to the conversation, and sends the updated context back to the LLM for the next step.

stem: Which of the following is an example of a tool an AI agent might use?

options.text: A web search function that takes a query string as input and returns a list of relevant URLs and snippets from the internet.
The softmax activation function applied to the final layer of the transformer to produce probability distributions over the vocabulary.
The attention mechanism that allows the model to weigh the importance of different tokens when generating each output token.
The tokeniser that converts raw text into integer IDs before they are passed into the model's embedding layer.

correct_answer: A web search function that takes a query string as input and returns a list of relevant URLs and snippets from the internet.

stem: What is the purpose of a human-in-the-loop mechanism in an AI agent workflow?

options.text: It pauses the agent at defined checkpoints so a human can review, approve, or redirect the agent's actions before execution continues, reducing the risk of irreversible errors.
It replaces the AI model entirely with a human operator who types responses manually, using the agent framework only for routing messages between users.
It ensures the agent runs faster by distributing computation across multiple human reviewers working in parallel on different subtasks.
It prevents the agent from accessing the internet by requiring a human to manually copy and paste web content into the context window.

correct_answer: It pauses the agent at defined checkpoints so a human can review, approve, or redirect the agent's actions before execution continues, reducing the risk of irreversible errors.

stem: In which scenario is a human-in-the-loop workflow most critical?

options.text: An agent that autonomously sends emails to thousands of customers on behalf of a company, where an error in tone or content could cause significant reputational damage.
An agent that generates draft social media captions for internal review, where a human will always see and approve the output before it is published.
An agent that formats a spreadsheet by applying a consistent number format to a column of prices in an offline document.
An agent that converts temperature values from Celsius to Fahrenheit using a deterministic mathematical formula with no external API calls.

correct_answer: An agent that autonomously sends emails to thousands of customers on behalf of a company, where an error in tone or content could cause significant reputational damage.

stem: What is the main trade-off when adding more human-in-the-loop checkpoints to an agent workflow?

options.text: More checkpoints increase oversight and reduce error risk, but they slow the workflow down and reduce the autonomy benefit that motivated using an agent in the first place.
More checkpoints always improve both speed and accuracy simultaneously, because humans correct model errors faster than the model can make them.
More checkpoints are only beneficial when the agent uses more than five tools; workflows with fewer tools should always run fully autonomously.
More checkpoints reduce the agent's context window usage, because each approval step clears the conversation history and starts a fresh session.

correct_answer: More checkpoints increase oversight and reduce error risk, but they slow the workflow down and reduce the autonomy benefit that motivated using an agent in the first place.

stem: Which of the following agent behaviours demonstrates full autonomy (no human in the loop)?

options.text: The agent researches, writes, and publishes a blog post directly to the company website without any human reviewing the content before it goes live.
The agent drafts a blog post and emails it to a content manager who must click Approve before the post is scheduled for publication.
The agent generates an outline and waits for the user to select which sections to expand before proceeding with the full draft.
The agent highlights sentences it is uncertain about and flags them for human review before submitting the document to the editor.

correct_answer: The agent researches, writes, and publishes a blog post directly to the company website without any human reviewing the content before it goes live.

stem: What is short-term memory in an AI agent context?

options.text: The current conversation history held in the context window, which is available during an active session but lost when the session ends.
A persistent database table that retains all conversations across every user session for the entire lifetime of the application.
The model's pre-trained weights, which store knowledge learned during training and remain fixed after deployment.
A hardware cache on the GPU that speeds up matrix multiplication during the transformer's attention computation.

correct_answer: The current conversation history held in the context window, which is available during an active session but lost when the session ends.

stem: Which of the following is an example of long-term memory in an AI agent system?

options.text: A vector database that stores summaries of past conversations and retrieves relevant ones at the start of each new session to give the agent historical context.
The list of messages in the current API call, passed as the messages array to the LLM endpoint for a single inference request.
The KV cache generated by the transformer during the forward pass, storing intermediate attention values for the current prompt.
The temperature and top-p parameters set by the developer to control the randomness of the model's output distribution.

correct_answer: A vector database that stores summaries of past conversations and retrieves relevant ones at the start of each new session to give the agent historical context.

stem: Why does an AI agent need explicit long-term memory mechanisms rather than relying solely on the context window?

options.text: Context windows have a finite token limit and are cleared between sessions, so information from past interactions is permanently lost unless actively stored externally.
Long-term memory mechanisms are required by law in GDPR-compliant applications to ensure all user data is retained indefinitely.
Context windows can only hold a single message at a time, so every response requires a separate database lookup to retrieve the previous message.
Long-term memory allows the agent to run faster by pre-computing all possible responses and caching them before the user asks a question.

correct_answer: Context windows have a finite token limit and are cleared between sessions, so information from past interactions is permanently lost unless actively stored externally.

stem: An agent is helping a user plan a trip over multiple sessions. The user mentioned their dietary restrictions in session 1. In session 3 the agent still remembers this. What mechanism made this possible?

options.text: Long-term memory: the dietary restriction was stored in a persistent store after session 1 and retrieved into the context at the start of session 3.
Short-term memory: the context window automatically retained all previous sessions without any explicit storage mechanism.
Model fine-tuning: the agent's weights were updated after session 1 to permanently encode the user's dietary preferences.
Prompt caching: the LLM provider cached the entire session 1 conversation and automatically prepended it to every subsequent API call.

correct_answer: Long-term memory: the dietary restriction was stored in a persistent store after session 1 and retrieved into the context at the start of session 3.
